chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from al-'Ala' from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a young boy marrying a young girl. He said: If it was their two parents who married them, then it is valid, but they have the option (of annulment) when they reach maturity. If they consent afterwards, then the dowry is upon the father. I said to him: Is the father's divorce of his son permissible during his minority? He said: No. This does not contradict the earlier narrations, because his saying 'but they have the option when they reach maturity' means that they have the right to annul the contract either by divorce from the side of the spouse or by the wife demanding what necessitates divorce and requires its annulment. And he did not mean by 'the option' here the ratification or invalidation of the contract such that the contract is suspended pending their choice. And that which reveals this is his saying in the narration: 'If it was their two parents who married them, then it is valid.' For if the contract were suspended pending their consent, there would be no difference between the parents and others, and it would be valid for others too. And it is established that there is a difference between the two cases, so it is known that the meaning is what we mentioned.

key_terms.الْخِيَارُ: option/right of choice (to ratify or annul)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal status of a marriage contracted by parents for a minor child, and does the child have the right to annul it upon reaching maturity?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Isfahani, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that while a father's marriage contract for his minor daughter is valid, it is not irrevocable; the daughter retains the right of *khiyar al-bulugh* (option of maturity) to ratify or annul it upon reaching puberty. The text distinguishes this from the father's unilateral right to divorce his minor son, explaining that the 'option' here refers to the daughter's power to demand dissolution or accept the contract, rather than the contract being merely suspended. This ruling underscores the Shia principle of protecting the minor's rights within the family structure, ensuring that parental authority does not override the child's consent upon maturity.
